o: Robots bounce off each other, but since robots are identical, a collision is equivalent to the two robots passing through each other and swapping labels. Therefore the multiset of positions after d seconds is obtained by simply moving each robot d units in its commanded direction, ignoring collisions entirely. In Example 1, final positions are [-2-3, 0-3, 2+3] = [-5,-3,5]; sorting gives [-5,-3,5], whose pair distances are 2+4+2 = 8, matching the expected output. We need the sum of |pi−pj| over all pairs of up to 1e5 points, which requires sorting plus a prefix-sum trick rather than an O(n²) double loop.
k: Collisions between identical robots are equivalent to passing through each other — directions can be ignored.
Sum of all pairwise distances on a line = Σ (i·a[i] − prefix of previous elements) after sorting.

a.n: Approach 1: Sort Final Positions + Prefix Sum
a.i: Compute each robot's final coordinate (x±d), sort them, and accumulate pairwise distances using the identity: for sorted array a, Σ_{j<i}(a[i]−a[j]) = Σ i·a[i] − running prefix sum.
s: Map each robot to its final position: +d for 'R', −d for 'L'.
Scan left to right keeping a running sum; add i·pos[i] − runningSum to the answer, modulo 1e9+7.
a.t: O(n log n) — dominated by sorting the final positions

w: Always use this pass-through trick for colliding identical particles. The main pitfalls are overflow (coordinates reach ±4e9, sums reach ~1e18, so use 64-bit integers and mod frequently) and forgetting to take mod of negative intermediate values in C++/Java. A follow-up might ask for individual trajectories — then label-swapping during collision matters.
